newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: New strike looms at Coal & Allied mine.
newsitem.headline: New strike looms at Coal & Allied mine.

text.p: The prospect of a renewed strike at Coal and Allied Industries Ltd's Hunter Valley No 1 coal mine loomed on Tuesday when the company announced it would introduce continuous production at the mine, north of Sydney.
A spokesman for the Construction, Forestry, Mining and Energy Union (CFMEU) told Reuters the move was a provocative action. "They want a knock-down drag-out fight," he said.

The decision was a clear breach of guidelines, with the CFMEU and Coal and Allied currently involved in a 21-day negotiating period as ordered by the Australian Industrial Relations Commission (AIRC), the spokesman said.

The AIRC recommended on August 12 that the companty and the CFMEU negotiate for a further 21 days after an earlier similar period expired without agreement. This followed a return to work by CFMEU miners after a six-week strike which ended on July 22.
The CFMEU would take the matter to Commissioner Greg Harrison of the AIRC, with meetings already in progress between the union and Harrison over Hunter Valley No. 1, the union official said.
CAIL, owned about 70 percent by Rio Tinto Plc/Ltd, produces about 25,000 tonnes of semi-soft coking and thermal coal a day for Japanese and other East Asian customers.
It lost production of about one million tonnes of coal in the last six-week strike, which ended on July 22. CAIL and the CFMEU have been negotiating since, as recommended by the AIRC.
The continuous production system had been in force until April but changed by CAIL itself, the CFMEU official also said.
CAIL had identified a minor but financially important work practice which was costing the mine millions of dollars a year in lost production, mine manager Allan Davies said in a statement.

From Tuesday the coal preparation plant would process coal continuously rather than stopping for up to 16 minutes during shift changes. "With three shifts per day we can improve production by 45 minutes per day," he said.
This would allow the company to produce an extra 200,000 tonnes of coal a year worth more than A$8 million, he said.
Overall CAIL believed it could double productivity through further changes to work practices, the CAIL spokesman said.
"Our belief in that was borne out during the strike, when with a rag-tag workforce of trainees and staff, production increased 75 percent in the six weeks," he said.
The A$8 million would go straight to the mine's bottom line, he added.
